opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a big part of it is just that switching has a real cost. Every one of these tools has its own quirks, and it takes a while to build intuition for how to work with it: how much context to give it, when to trust it, when it's about to go off the rails, how to break up a task so it succeeds. I've built up that intuition with Claude Code, and it's good enough for almost everything I do day to day, so the marginal benefit of trying yet another tool usually doesn't justify the time.

Also, things move so fast that if you try to keep up with every release, you could spend all your time evaluating tools rather than doing research. One is better this month, another is better next month, and the differences at any given moment are often smaller than the online discussion makes them seem. As a researcher, what I care about is getting my experiments done and testing my ideas. So I'd rather go deep with one tool that works well, and I'll only reconsider if I keep hearing from people I trust that something else is dramatically better, or if I hit a wall.

I think there's a human habit element too, right? It's like your editor or your programming language. Once you're comfortable and it fits your workflow, you stick with it. I'm sure I miss out on some things by not trying everything, but I'm okay with that trade-off.

r001.rationale: The candidate says switching tools has a learning cost and that focusing on Claude Code has built useful intuition, avoiding effort spent evaluating competing tools.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, a lot of it comes down to time. I'm an assistant professor now, so my day is split between advising students, teaching, writing grants, and the small amount of actual research time I can protect. Every new tool has a learning curve, and the cost isn't just the hour you spend setting it up, it's the week where you're slightly less productive because your habits don't match the tool yet. Switching between three or four of these things means you're paying that cost constantly and never getting really good at any of them.

With Claude Code I decided early on to just commit. I learned its quirks, how to prompt it for the kind of work I do, where it's reliable and where I need to check every line. Once you have that model of the tool in your head, you can move fast. You know when to trust it to refactor a data loader and when to watch it carefully because it's touching a loss function. That intuition is worth more to me than whatever marginal gain I'd get from benchmarking the alternatives.

The other thing is that the workflow fits how I actually work. I'm mostly in the terminal, mostly in a repo with a lot of existing code, and I want something that reads the codebase and makes changes in place rather than something I have to copy snippets in and out of. It handles that well. It also runs the experiments, looks at the output, and iterates, which is close to how I'd work with a student.

I'll say I'm not dogmatic about it. If one of my students shows me a tool that does something clearly better, I'll look at it. But the research I care about, understanding architectures, understanding what makes these models work, that's where I want my attention. The coding tool is infrastructure. I want it to be boring and dependable, and then get out of the way.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he committed to Claude Code, learned its quirks and reliability, and avoids the ongoing learning costs of switching among several tools.
